    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35487v1</id>
    <title>A Mathematical Murmuration</title>
    <updated>2026-10-26T14:15:10Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35487v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.35487v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We give a summary of a large group activity presented to primary school children as part of a STEAM (STEM plus The Arts) event. We describe the routine we demonstrated, this was based upon the tutting dance form, and the murmuration of starlings. Indeed, this demonstrates movement/dance as both a viable and engaging form of teaching mathematics.</summary>

  <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35263v1</id>
    <title>On AI and Progress in Mathematics: Dreaming a Mathematical Universal Machine</title>
    <updated>2026-10-26T11:43:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35263v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.35263v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In the autumn of 2026, mathematics is facing what may be the deepest crisis in its history. The entire ecosystem through which mathematical knowledge is produced, validated, communicated, and assessed is beginning to break down. Mathematics departments, those usually quiet and civilized places, are suddenly in turmoil -- the unlikely theaters of a new Battle of the Ancients and the Moderns. The source of the crisis is clear: AI systems have become better than even the best human mathematicians at proving and validating mathematical results. This document proposes a metaphor for mathematical activity: we once thought of ourselves as mountain climbers; soon, we may become miners digging in the mathematical mine, either collaborating or competing with mathematical AI machines. Publications would then be seen primarily as a means of helping humans understand mathematics, while the measurement of mathematical progress would be entrusted to a Mathematical Universal Machine. In nontechnical terms, we explore what this brave new world of mathematics might look like and how we might collectively shape its future.</summary>
    <category term="math.HO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

  <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34803v1</id>
    <title>An event is a set, not a number: building the algebra of events before the probability measure in a school progression</title>
    <updated>2026-10-26T03:42:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34803v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.34803v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Asked what an event is, pupils often answer with a fraction. This paper argues that school probability should separate two learnings and order them: the algebra of events (random experiment, outcomes, sample space, events as sets of outcomes, the operations not, or, and) and the probability measure, which attaches a number to each event. Before learning to compute the probability of an event, pupils should learn to build, identify and handle the event. The thesis rests on the structure of finite probability, in which the rules are facts about events carried over by an additive function, and on the history of the subject, in which errors such as d'Alembert's two tosses concerned the weighting of outcomes and were resolved by refining events into equally likely outcomes. Five design principles are stated: two objects with two names; the event before its probability; modal judgements (certain, possible, impossible) on sets before numbers; the algebra of events taught as such, with the rules derived from it; the sample space as a modelling choice, with frequencies last, as statistical estimates, and the separation repeated for conditional probability and random variables. They are confronted with the probability chapters, from age 9 to 18, of the French-curriculum courses published at https://commeunjeu.org, with research and other curricula. In primary school events precede probabilities without set notation, which comes at age 12; the lessons apply the principles and prove the rules from events in lower secondary school. But, in the version analysed, events account for 18 to 44 percent of the exercises, proofs are hidden in upper secondary school, and automatically corrected calculations record only the number. It proposes number-free tasks on events for ages 6 to 8 and changes to the International Baccalaureate curriculum. No empirical evaluation is reported; hypotheses are stated.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34546v1</id>
    <title>Experimental Mathematics: Discovering The Half-Derivative from First Principles</title>
    <updated>2026-10-25T20:15:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34546v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.34546v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This expository paper grew out of two lectures in Miller's Math 409: The little Questions (Williams College, Fall 2026). We explore fractional derivatives by asking what a ``half-derivative'' might mean if applying it twice is to recover an ordinary derivative. Linearity and a natural guess for the half-derivative of a power function lead to a functional equation related to the classical factorial recurrence. Choosing the familiar Gamma-function extension gives the classical formula \[
  \mathscr{D}^{1/2}(x^n)
  \ =\ \frac{Γ(n+1)}{Γ(n+\tfrac12)}x^{n-1/2}. \] We derive $Γ(n+1)=n!$, evaluate $Γ(1/2)=\sqrtπ$ using the Gaussian integral, and verify the half-derivative formula with an elementary integral. Along the way, we explore how the Gamma function generalizes factorials and binomial coefficients beyond their classical domains, encounter the double factorial, see why the usual product rule fails, and examine the half-derivative of $e^x$. We also explain why the original requirements do not determine a unique operator. The treatment emphasizes motivation, the benefits of experimentation through accessible calculations in test cases, rather than the general theory of fractional calculus.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33975v1</id>
    <title>A Pythagoras Tree Grown from a Dodecahedron</title>
    <updated>2026-10-25T01:15:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33975v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.33975v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Pythagoras tree of A. E. Bosman (1942) is drawn with squares in the plane and, in the three-dimensional versions we know of, with cubes. This article documents a tree built instead from regular dodecahedra: each dodecahedron carries five smaller copies, one on each edge of a single pentagonal "crown" face, scaled by $g \approx 0.4346$ and twisted by $45^\circ$ about the edge. The construction first existed only as a pair of rendered images and two undocumented C++ programs. We recover its exact parameters from the original Blender scene, reformulate it as an iterated function system with condensation, and prove with a short computer-assisted argument that it never collides with itself: two of its dodecahedra overlap only when one is the parent of the other. A Pythagorean identity for the six face axes of the dodecahedron singles out the scale $1/\sqrt{5}$ and the twist $\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})$. With these values each child rests flat against a face of its parent, the five children together have exactly the parent's surface area, and the crown of the tree is a fractal of Hausdorff dimension exactly 2. Finally we ask whether the tree can grow on all twelve faces at once. A parity argument shows that at the artwork's proportions it cannot, but smaller scale factors admit certified clash-free all-faces trees.</summary>
